summary:
Legal gender recognition in Switzerland rests on self-declaration. Since 1 January 2022 any person registered in a Swiss municipality may change their sex marker and/or first name by personal declaration before a civil registrar, with no surgical requirement and no court proceeding. In the first months of the route about 350 people had used it.

The treatment of minors is contested between the chambers of the Federal Assembly. The National Council removed the requirement for guardian consent for 12 to 18-year-olds, while the Council of States set 16 as the age below which guardian consent is needed; the wording finally in force is not resolved by the available sources.

Same-sex marriage has been in force since 1 July 2022 under the 'Marriage for All' reform, which also opened adoption and IVF to same-sex couples; the reform was approved by 64.1% of voters in referendum.

Public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been punishable under Article 261bis of the Criminal Code since 1 July 2020. That provision does not reach gender identity, so a person targeted specifically for being trans does not receive the criminal-law aggravation available on sexual-orientation grounds. Switzerland has no general hate-crime provision, and hate crimes are handled through the anti-discrimination article instead.

Reported anti-LGBTIQ+ violence is rising. Monitoring by the LGBTIQ Helpline records roughly six hate crimes per week, 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020. On 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons 2026-2030, built on support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence, and coordinated by the Federal Office for Gender Equality. The OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report for Switzerland notes that recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes and that police do not record bias motivation.

Placement of trans detainees is a cantonal matter. There is no federal provision on trans placement in detention and no Swiss case law on the subject; the canton of Basel-Stadt inserted an explicit gender-identity clause into its detention law (JVG) on 13 November 2019, requiring that the gender identity of the detained person be respected as far as possible and allowing the prison directorate to deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority.

Employment protection is stronger than the criminal-law picture suggests. Employers must safeguard employees' personal dignity under Articles 328ff. of the Code of Obligations, concretised for trans people by the Equality Act (GLG), and trans staff may use their preferred name and gender at work without any official document change. In June 2023 the Federal Supreme Court upheld a cantonal school's dismissal of a teacher who refused to call a transgender student by his chosen male first name, ruling that the school's duty to protect the student's privacy and self-determination outweighed the teacher's religious objections.

UNHCR's Switzerland guidance records that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited and that same-sex couples have been able to marry since 1 July 2022.
tangentialFactors:
LegalClarity's June 2026 assessment of Swiss LGBT rights runs from marriage equality to gender recognition while stating that gaps remain, and its framing is consistent with the pattern above: recognition and relationship law are settled, criminal-law protection is not symmetric across protected grounds.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map country page publishes an overall index score and per-category compliance ratings for Switzerland, assessed after the 2021 self-determination and discrimination votes, which gives visitors a comparative benchmark against neighbouring systems.

Conversion therapy remains unregulated at federal level: the National Council adopted a national ban on 12 December 2022 by 143 votes to 37 with 11 abstentions, but the bill is still pending in the Council of States. Cantonal bans exist in Neuchâtel (2023), Valais and Vaud (2024). The Federal Council states that such therapies are ineffective and cause significant suffering to young people subjected to them, and that they would breach professional duties, while leaving further federal regulation open as of a 2026 report.

Blood donation rules moved on 1 November 2023 to a four-month deferral after last new sexual contact for gay men, down from the one-year deferral in force since 2017.
localsOnly:
Resident workers can invoke Articles 328ff. of the Code of Obligations together with the Equality Act (GLG), which requires employers to protect personal dignity and gives trans employees the right to use their preferred name and gender at work without a preceding legal name change.

Support infrastructure is established and domestic: a helpline launched by Swiss LGBT groups in November 2016, Dialogai (founded 1982) offering helplines and advice, and Transgender Network Switzerland advising on legal sex and name changes, the armed forces and asylum. The LGBTIQ Helpline also monitors reported hate crimes.

Residents in Neuchâtel, Valais and Vaud are protected by cantonal conversion-therapy bans, while elsewhere the practice is not prohibited by statute; the national ban passed by the National Council in December 2022 has not completed its passage.

Detention conditions for trans residents are governed by cantonal legislation, which is where placement rules such as Basel-Stadt's 2019 gender-identity clause are set and where any challenge would arise.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the final wording on guardian consent for minors changing legal sex. The National Council struck the consent requirement and the Council of States fixed 16 as the threshold; the sources do not confirm which text was adopted in the final law.

Unresolved: whether Switzerland has any federal rule on the placement of trans prisoners. The available sources record no federal provision and no case law, and describe placement practice as cantonal, so a visitor's placement in custody cannot be predicted from national sources.

Not sourced: a gender-identity equivalent of Article 261bis. The inventory states the provision covers sexual orientation only, and nothing indicates a trans-specific criminal-law protection.

Unresolved: whether the 2026 National Action Plan has produced measurable change in recording or victim support. Adoption is documented; outcome data is not.

The hate-crime figures come from NGO helpline monitoring rather than official police statistics, and OSCE/ODIHR records that police do not capture bias motivation, so official counts understate the picture.

School-level data in the sources is a single 2018 survey of 1,700 Neuchâtel schoolchildren aged 14-15 (10% of girls and 5% of boys identifying as LGBT, 38% reporting slaps, kicks or punches, 25% frequent harassment, 16% physical violence, 7% discrimination by a teacher) and cannot be generalised to the country.
